elements.quote: Weincludedrandomisedtrials in people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19 that compared blood products and covid-19-specific antiviral antibodies against one another or against no intervention, placebo, or standard care.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the population (people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19), the interventions (blood products and covid-19-specific antiviral antibodies), and the comparators (one another, no intervention, placebo, or standard care), which provides the planned comparisons consistent with a PICO-style specification.

elements.quote: We included randomised trials in people with suspected, probable, or confirmed covid-19 that compared blood products and covid-19-specific antiviral antibodies against one another or against no intervention, placebo, or standard care. We included trials regardless of publication status (peer reviewed, in press, or preprint) or language. No restrictions were applied based on severity of illness or setting. For each eligible trial, pairs of reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, extract data independently using a standardised, pilot tested data extraction form. Reviewers collect information on trial characteristics (trial registration, publication status, study status, design), patient characteristics (country, age, sex, smoking habits, comorbidities, setting and type of care, severity of covid-19 symptoms, timing of therapy relative to symptom onset), donor characteristics (selection criteria, sex, severity of disease), and outcomes of interest (means or medians and measures of variability for continuous outcomes and the number of participants analysed and the number of participants who experienced an event for dichotomous outcomes). We excluded randomised trials evaluating vaccines, pharmacologic drugs, nutrition, traditional Chinese herbal medicines, and non-drug supportive care interventions. We identified and separately categorised trials including patients with covid-19 that evaluated these interventions. Randomised trials evaluating drug treatments and prophylaxis for covid-19 were synthesised in separate living network meta-analyses. We excluded non-randomised trials.
elements.reason: Explicit specification of population (suspected/probable/confirmed), eligible study design (randomised trials), interventions and comparators, exclusions (vaccines, drugs, non-randomised trials), settings/severity (no restrictions), and many trial/patient/donor characteristics used to determine eligibility.

elements.quote: We included trials regardless of publication status (peer reviewed, in press, or preprint) or language.
elements.reason: The review specifies publication/report status and language eligibility but does not state any dissemination year restrictions; thus report-characteristic criteria are partially specified.
No explicit statement distinguishing exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported is present in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We performed bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis for outcomes with sufficient data, and synthesise all other outcomes using pairwise bayesian random-effects meta-analyses if there was only one comparison for a specific outcome.
elements.reason: The methods state which synthesis methods will be used (network or pairwise) and text_15 defines the comparisons (blood products and antiviral antibodies versus each other or versus no intervention/placebo/standard care), but the evidence does not explicitly map each named group to the specific syntheses or link every synthesis grouping to the review objectives in a detailed way.

elements.quote: We utilised a comprehensive literature search without any restrictions on language or publication status, explicit eligibility criteria, and limited meta-analysis of interventions that were randomised to at least 100 patients (or had ≥20 events) to avoid spurious or imprecise findings with network meta-analysis.
elements.reason: Provides a rationale for a notable restriction (threshold for conducting meta-analysis: ≥100 patients or ≥20 events) explaining it was to avoid spurious or imprecise findings.

elements.quote: We searched WHO information sources from 1 December 2019 to 21 July 2021, and the Chinese literature from inception to 20 February 2021.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the dates on which WHO information sources and Chinese literature searches were last conducted.

elements.reason: The names of many bibliographic databases are listed, but the manuscript does not report the search interface/platform for each database nor the coverage dates for each individual database.

elements.reason: The manuscript lists and defines the outcome domains sought, providing a detailed list of outcomes.

elements.quote: across the following domains: bias arising from the randomisation process; bias owing to departures from the intended intervention; bias from missing outcome data; bias in measurement of the outcome; bias in selection of the reported results, including deviations from the registered protocol; bias due to competing risks; and bias arising from early termination for benefit.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists the specific domains assessed by the risk-of-bias tool.

elements.quote: We rate trials at high risk of bias overall if one or more domains were rated as (c) someconcerns, probably high risk of bias or as (d) high risk of bias, and as low risk of bias overall if all domains were rated as ( b ) some concerns, probably low risk of bias or ( a ) low risk of bias.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that an overall risk-of-bias judgement was made and specifies the rules used to derive high or low overall risk.

elements.quote: We assessed risk of bias using a modification of the Cochrane risk of bias 2.0 tool.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that a modification/adaptation of RoB 2.0 was used but does not describe what adaptations were made or provide details of those changes.

elements.quote: For each eligible trial and outcome, reviewers, following training and calibration exercises, use ... Reviewers resolve discrepancies by discussion and, when necessary, with adjudication by a third party.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes reviewer training, discrepancy resolution (discussion and third-party adjudication), and that reviewers assessed studies, but does not state the exact number of reviewers per study or explicitly state whether assessments were performed independently.
No information is provided about processes to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators.
No description of any automation tools used for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) is provided.

elements.quote: Wesummarisedtheeffectofinterventionsondichotomousoutcomes using odds ratios and their corresponding 95% credible interval (CI). For outcomes with extremely rare events, we summarised the effect of interventions using risk difference and 95% CI. For continuous outcomes, specifically duration of hospital stay, we used the mean difference and corresponding 95% CI ... For time to symptom resolution, time to viral clearance, and duration of mechanical ventilation, we performed the analyses using ratio of means and corresponding 95% CI before calculating the mean difference in days
elements.reason: Specifies effect measures for dichotomous outcomes (odds ratios; risk difference for extremely rare events), continuous outcomes (mean difference), and time-to/event measures (ratio of means then mean difference in days).

elements.quote: In the absence of data from quantitative studies of patient values, the review team chose thresholds of small but important effects by consensus: 1% for mortality, 2% for mechanical ventilation, 1% for hospitalisation, 1 day for duration of hospitalisation, and 2% for all adverse effects.
elements.reason: Reports explicit thresholds for interpreting effect sizes (small but important effects) and notes these were chosen by consensus in absence of patient-values data, providing rationale.

elements.quote: To facilitate interpretation of results of dichotomous outcomes, we calculated absolute effects per 1000 patients. ... For time to symptom resolution, time to viral clearance, and duration of mechanical ventilation, we performed the analyses using ratio of means and corresponding 95% CI before calculating the mean difference in days
elements.reason: Describes re-expression methods: converting relative measures to absolute effects per 1000 patients and converting ratio-of-means results into mean difference in days.

elements.quote: For continuous outcomes, specifically duration of hospital stay, we used the mean difference and corresponding 95% CI because we expect similar durations across randomised trials. For outcomes with extremely rare events, we summarised the effect of interventions using risk difference and 95% CI.
elements.reason: Provides justification for choice of effect measures (mean difference because durations expected similar across trials; risk difference for extremely rare events).

elements.quote: We meta-analysed interventions with ≥100 patients randomised or ≥20 events per treatment arm.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies quantitative thresholds used to decide which interventions were pooled in meta-analyses (≥100 patients randomized or ≥20 events per arm). Additional supporting text (text_20) clarifies that network meta-analysis was used for outcomes with sufficient data and pairwise meta-analysis when only one comparison existed, indicating explicit processes for determining eligibility for each synthesis.

elements.quote: For outcomes where the median risk of an event in the control group was 0 (that is, TACO, TRALI, adverse events leading to discontinuation), we performed network meta-analysis with risk difference and fixed effects rather than odd ratios and random effects. ... Wedid not perform any adjustments for interventions with zero events. The R code used is available publicly at https://github.com/covid19lnma/covid19_lnma/.
elements.reason: Describes specific data-preparation decisions for synthesis (choice of effect measure and model when control event risk was 0; statement about not adjusting zero-event interventions) and provides analysis code link.

elements.quote: Table 1 presents the characteristics of the included studies. The supplementary data on bmj.com present additional study characteristics, outcome data, and risk of bias assessments for each study.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that Table 1 displays study characteristics and that supplementary tables present additional study characteristics and outcome data, describing the tabular structures used to display results.

elements.quote: We created network plots using the networkplot commandofStataversion15.1(StataCorp,CollegeStation,TX,USA). Thickness of lines between nodes and the size of nodes were based on the inverse variance of the direct comparison. 32
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the graphical methods used (network plots via Stata networkplot) and how visual elements (line thickness and node size) were determined; other text (text_27) also notes forest plots and figure summaries.

elements.quote: Treatments were grouped into nodes based on intervention, not dose or duration.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the basis for grouping studies within the network plots (grouped by intervention rather than dose or duration).
No evidence was found describing a rationale for using non-standard graphs or explaining why such graphs were chosen.

elements.quote: Weperformed a random-effects bayesian meta-analysis using the bayesmeta package 29 in RStudio version 3.5.3 (R Studio, Boston, MA, USA). ... Network meta-analysis was performed using the R package gemtc. Weused three Markov chains with 100 000 iterations after an initial burn-in of 10 000 and a thinning of 10. ... The R code used is available publicly at https://github.com/covid19lnma/covid19_lnma/.
elements.reason: Software and packages (bayesmeta, gemtc) and RStudio version are explicitly reported, with MCMC settings and link to code.

elements.quote: Weperformed bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis for outcomes with sufficient data, and synthesise all other outcomes using pairwise bayesian random-effects meta-analyses if there was only one comparison for a specific outcome. 29
elements.reason: The authors state that when data were insufficient for network meta-analysis they used pairwise Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses, describing the alternative synthesis approach.

elements.quote: Weperformed a random-effects bayesian meta-analysis using the bayesmeta package 29 in RStudio version 3.5.3 (R Studio, Boston, MA, USA). As suggested in an empirical study, we used a plausible prior for the variance parameter and a uniform prior for the effect parameter. 33 For outcomes where the median risk of an event in the control group was 0 (that is, TACO, TRALI, adverse events leading to discontinuation), we performed network meta-analysis with risk difference and fixed effects rather than odd ratios and random effects.
elements.reason: The model types (Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis; for certain zero-event outcomes, network meta-analysis with risk difference and fixed effects) and rationale (control median risk 0 led to choice of risk difference/fixed effects; prior choices justified by empirical study) are described.

elements.quote: Weperformed a random-effects bayesian meta-analysis using the bayesmeta package 29 in RStudio version 3.5.3 (R Studio, Boston, MA, USA). ... Network meta-analysis was performed using the R package gemtc. Weused three Markov chains with 100 000 iterations after an initial burn-in of 10 000 and a thinning of 10.
elements.reason: The statistical method is described as Bayesian meta-analysis with MCMC implementation details (package, chains, iterations, burn-in, thinning).

elements.quote: Node splitting models were used to obtain indirect estimates and to assess local heterogeneity. 34
elements.reason: Methods to assess local heterogeneity/inconsistency are reported (node splitting models).
No between-study variance estimator (e.g., tau2 estimator name) for random-effects meta-analysis is reported in the supplied evidence.
The method used to calculate confidence/credible intervals for the summary effect is not described in the provided text.

elements.quote: Weused three Markov chains with 100 000 iterations after an initial burn-in of 10 000 and a thinning of 10. ... We did not perform any adjustments for interventions with zero events. The R code used is available publicly at https://github.com/covid19lnma/covid19_lnma/.
elements.reason: Additional random-effects/Bayesian implementation details are provided (MCMC chains, iterations, burn-in, thinning), statement about zero-event adjustments, and availability of code.

elements.quote: As suggested in an empirical study, we used a plausible prior for the variance parameter and a uniform prior for the effect parameter. 33
elements.reason: Priors for the variance parameter and effect parameter are explicitly described.

elements.quote: Weperformed bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis for outcomes with sufficient data, and synthesise all other outcomes using pairwise bayesian random-effects meta-analyses if there was only one comparison for a specific outcome. 29
elements.reason: The authors identify that network meta-analysis was used only for outcomes with sufficient data and describe using pairwise meta-analysis when network synthesis was not appropriate (insufficient data).

elements.quote: We plan to conduct subgroup analyses based on high versus low risk of bias studies. Additionally, for convalescent plasma, we plan to perform subgroup analyses based on antibody titres and time of infusion relative to disease progression.
elements.reason: The methods to explore heterogeneity (planned subgroup analyses) are explicitly specified, including risk of bias and subgroup factors for convalescent plasma.

elements.quote: Additionally, for convalescent plasma, we plan to perform subgroup analyses based on antibody titres and time of infusion relative to disease progression. We hypothesise that treatment with convalescent plasma will be more efficacious when transfusion occurs earlier in the disease course, and when plasma from patients with more severe illness is used.
elements.reason: The factors (antibody titres; time of infusion), implied factor levels (earlier vs later infusion; plasma from more severe illness vs less), and an expected direction of effect modification (more efficacious earlier and with plasma from more severe illness) are reported.
No statement specifies whether subgroup/meta-regression analyses will use study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.

elements.quote: When there is statistical evidence of a subgroup effect, we will assess its credibility using the Instrument to assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses in randomised controlled trials and meta-analyses (ICEMAN) tool.
elements.reason: The authors state the method (ICEMAN) they will use to assess the credibility of observed subgroup effects, which addresses how subgroup effects will be evaluated/compared.
No informal methods for exploring heterogeneity when meta-analysis is unsuitable (including factors and levels) are described in the provided evidence.
There is no identification in the provided text of analyses that were not pre-specified (no statement labeling any heterogeneity analyses as post-hoc).
No text in the provided evidence describes any sensitivity analyses or details of sensitivity analyses conducted to assess robustness of synthesized results.
No text in the provided evidence identifies any sensitivity analyses, pre-specified or post-hoc, so there is no information identifying non‑pre-specified sensitivity analyses.
